Efficient Federated RLHF via Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization

Deyi Wang ††thanks: Both authors contributed equally to this research. Affiliation: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor Email: deyiwang@umich.edu    Qining Zhang11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor Email: qiningz@umich.edu    Lei Ying Affiliation: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor Email: leiying@umich.edu
Abstract

This paper considers reinforcement learning from human feedback in a federated learning setting with resource-constrained agents, such as edge devices. We propose an efficient federated RLHF algorithm, named Partitioned, Sign-based Stochastic Zeroth-order Policy Optimization (Par-S2ZPO). The algorithm is built on zeroth-order optimization with binary perturbation, resulting in low communication, computation, and memory complexity by design. Our theoretical analysis establishes an upper bound on the convergence rate of Par-S2ZPO, revealing that it is as efficient as its centralized counterpart in terms of sample complexity but converges faster in terms of policy update iterations. Our experimental results show that it outperforms a FedAvg-based RLHF on four MuJoCo RL tasks.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a cornerstone for fine-tuning LLMs [14, 16] and advancing physical intelligence in robotics [5, 7]. This paper considers RLHF in a federated learning setting, in which multiple resource-constrained agents (e.g., edge devices) collaborate to train an RL model using human preferences. Implementing existing federated algorithms, such as FedAvg [12], for this purpose requires frequent computation and exchanges of a large amount of gradient information, and is therefore challenging when edge devices have limited memory, computation, and communication resources. For example, fine-tuning an LLM involves the gradients of billions of model parameters, which could exceed the communication and computing capacity of an edge device. Even when such fine-tuning is feasible, it may also quickly drain the battery.

In this paper, we propose a federated RLHF algorithm, named Partitioned, Sign-based Stochastic Zeroth-order Policy Optimization, or Par-S2ZPO for short. It is efficient in communication, computation, and memory by design, based on the following key ideas:

  • •

    Zeroth-order optimization with binary perturbation: Par-S2ZPO uses the following sign-based, two-point, zeroth-order method to approximate the direction of the gradient:

    ∇𝜽V​(π𝜽)≈c0​𝔼𝒗​[sign⁡[V⁡(π𝜽+μ​𝒗)−V⁡(π𝜽)]​𝒗],\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V(\pi_{\bm{\theta}})\approx c_{0}~\mathbb{E}_{\bm{v}}\left[\sign[V(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\bm{v}}})-V(\pi_{\bm{\theta}})]{\bm{v}}\right],

    where π𝜽\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}} is the current policy parameterized by a parameter 𝜽{\bm{\theta}}, π𝜽+μ​𝒗\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\bm{v}}} is a perturbed policy obtained by perturbing the policy parameter with a direction 𝒗{\bm{v}} and distance μ\mu, and c0c_{0} is an absolute constant. To reduce communication and memory complexity, Par-S2ZPO uses binary perturbations, in which each entry is either +1+1 or −1-1, so vv can be stored and communicated easily.

  • •

    Partitioned RLHF: To further reduce the memory requirement at each agent, Par-S2ZPO partitions the policy parameters into KK subsets, where KK is the number of agents. Each agent perturbs only the parameter subset assigned to them: that is, for agent k,k, the perturbed policy has parameter 𝜽+μ​𝒗k,{{\bm{\theta}}}+\mu{\bm{v}}_{k}, where the ii-th element of 𝒗k{\bm{v}}_{k} is the ii-th element of 𝒗{\bm{v}} only if the this parameter entry is assigned to agent kk. Otherwise, it is 00. For example, if the actor is a neural network with m​KmK layers, then Par-S2ZPO assigns mm layers to each agent.

  • •

    Binary feedback: After agent kk compares the current policy with its perturbed policy from human feedback, the agent communicates only a binary value O^k∈{−1,+1}\hat{O}_{k}\in\{-1,+1\} indicating whether 𝒗k{\bm{v}}_{k} is a favorable perturbation direction, incuring minimal communication overhead. The policy is moved toward direction 𝒈^=∑kO^k​𝒗k\hat{{\bm{g}}}=\sum_{k}\hat{O}_{k}{\bm{v}}_{k} with a properly chosen learning rate α\alpha.

1.1 Main Contributions

The key contributions of this paper are summarized below.

Efficient Algorithm Design.

Assume the parameterized policy consists of dd parameters, i.e., 𝜽∈ℝd,{\bm{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},. During each policy update, Par-S2ZPO requires only d+Kd+K bits of communication, each agent needs to store only an additional d/Kd/K parameters besides the current policy, and furthermore, no gradient calculation is needed. Therefore, Par-S2ZPO is communication-, computation-, and memory-efficient.

Provable Rate of Convergence.

To understand its performance, we theoretically analyze the convergence of Par-S2ZPO and establish an upper bound on the convergence rate. From the upper bound, we have two key observations:

  • •

    When fixing the total number of trajectories for human evaluations during training, which can be regarded as the sample complexity of the algorithm, the upper bound is independent of K.K. In other words, sample-wise, a KK-agent system is as efficient as a centralized, single-agent system (K=1K=1), even when the single-agent system takes KK times more iterations under the same sample complexity. Our simulations will confirm this observation.

  • •

    There is a tradeoff in choosing the batch size for obtaining human preference feedback because a large batch size results in more accurate evaluations from human evaluators, but a smaller number of training iterations. In practice, this is an important hyperparameter that should be chosen carefully based on the environment.

Numerical Evaluation.

Empirically, we implemented Par-S2ZPO in four MuJoCo RL environments, evaluated its performance with different KKs, and compared it with FedAvg-based zeroth-order policy optimization. Par-S2ZPO outperforms the FedAvg-based algorithm in all four environments.

1.2 Related Work

The proposed Par-S2ZPO is related to several research areas.

RLHF and preference-based RL: RLHF methods, such as InstructGPT [14] and DPO [16], have become a cornerstone of post-training for large language models (LLMs). Recently, zeroth-order methods such as ZPG [22] and ZSPO [21] have also been proposed for RLHF in general MDPs. ZPG [22] estimates value differences from human preferences and combines them with zeroth-order gradient approximation, whereas ZSPO [21] only estimates the sign of the value difference via human preferences, so it works for unknown preference models (link functions). Par-S2ZPO extends zeroth-order policy optimization to the federated setting. Unlike ZSPO and ZPG, which use real-valued perturbation vectors (e.g., Gaussian or uniform), Par-S2ZPO uses Rademacher perturbations ({−1,+1}\{-1,+1\}) to reduce communication, computation, and memory costs. As a result, its convergence analysis differs.

Federated Learning (FL) and Split Learning (SL): FL [12] enables multiple agents to collaboratively train a model while keeping data local. In FedAvg [12], the central server updates the global model by aggregating local updates from all agents. FedBCD [11] adopts a block-coordinate training strategy, in which each agent updates only a subset of the model parameters. Split Learning (SL) [19] goes one step further by partitioning a model into multiple components and storing only one component at each agent, and requires sequential communication across the split model during training. Similar to FedBCD [11], Par-S2ZPO partitions the parameter set into subsets. Unlike FedBCD [11] and SL [19], Par-S2ZPO uses zeroth-order policy optimization with binary perturbations rather than gradient-based updates, thereby reducing computation and communication overhead.

Sign-based Zeroth-Order Optimization: Sign-based methods, such as sign-GD [9], estimate coordinate-wise gradient signs and use them to optimize the objective. In contrast, Par-S2ZPO uses binary perturbations together with preference feedback to infer a policy-improvement direction from human preferences. Therefore, the “sign” used in Par-S2ZPO is conceptually different from sign-GD.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the problem setting, the partitioned federated learning scheme, and the necessary notations.

2.1 Preference-based Reinforcement Learning

We first present the model of the episodic RL problem, and then introduce the preference feedback mechanism.

Episodic RL. An episodic RL problem is represented by a finite-horizon Markov decision process ℳ=(𝕊,𝔸,H,𝑷,𝝁0)\mathcal{M}=({\mathbb{S}},{\mathbb{A}},H,{\bm{P}},{\bm{\mu}}_{0}), where 𝕊{\mathbb{S}} is the state space and 𝔸{\mathbb{A}} is the action space, both may be uncountable. HH is the planning horizon, 𝑷={𝑷h}h=1H{\bm{P}}=\{{\bm{P}}_{h}\}_{h=1}^{H} is the set of transition kernels, and 𝝁0{\bm{\mu}}_{0} is the initial distribution of states. At the start of each episode tt, the agent chooses a policy πt\pi_{t} which is represented as a set of functions {πt,h:𝕊→𝒫⁡(𝔸)}h=1H\{\pi_{t,h}:{\mathbb{S}}\to\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{A}})\}_{h=1}^{H}, where 𝒫⁡(𝔸)\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{A}}) denotes the set of all probability distributions over the action space. Then an initial state st,1s_{t,1} is sampled from the initial distribution 𝝁0{\bm{\mu}}_{0}. At each step hh, the agent observes the current state st,hs_{t,h} and then takes an action at,h=πh​(st,h)a_{t,h}=\pi_{h}(s_{t,h}) according to the chosen policy. The environment consequently moves to a new state st,h+1s_{t,h+1} sampled from the distribution 𝑷h(⋅|st,h,at,h).{\bm{P}}_{h}(\cdot|s_{t,h},a_{t,h}). For each trajectory τt={(st,h,at,h)}h=1H\tau_{t}=\{(s_{t,h},a_{t,h})\}_{h=1}^{H} generated by the agent at episode tt, we assume the expected return r⁡(τt)∈[0,H]r(\tau_{t})\in[0,H] is a general function determined by the entire trajectory and may not be possible to be decomposable into per-step rewards as in traditional RL. For any policy π\pi, we define the value function as J⁡(π)=𝔼s∼𝝁0​[Vπ​(s)]J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim{\bm{\mu}}_{0}}[V^{\pi}(s)] where Vπ​(s)V^{\pi}(s) is the expected reward of trajectories starting from ss and using policy π\pi:

Vπ​(s)=\displaystyle V^{\pi}(s)= 𝔼π[r(τ)|s1=s]=𝔼[r(τ)|s1=s,{a1,⋯,aH}∼π].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\left.r(\tau)\right|s_{1}=s]=\mathbb{E}[\left.r(\tau)\right|s_{1}=s,\{a_{1},\cdots,a_{H}\}\sim\pi].

Policy Parameterization and Optimization. We consider parametrized policies, represented as a function class 𝒩={π𝜽:𝕊×[H]→𝒫(𝔸)|𝜽∈ℝd}{\mathcal{N}}=\{\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}:{\mathbb{S}}\times[H]\to\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{A}})|{\bm{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\}, which takes a step hh and state ss as input, and outputs the probability distribution of the next action. For example, 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} may be the weights of an actor network. Each parameter 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} induces a policy denoted as π𝜽\pi_{\bm{\theta}}. Our goal is to find the best parameter 𝜽∗{\bm{\theta}}^{*} to maximize the expected value function over the initial state distribution, i.e.,

max𝜽∈ℝd⁡V⁡(π𝜽)=𝔼s∼𝝁0​[Vπ𝜽​(s)].\max_{{\bm{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}V(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}})=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim{\bm{\mu}}_{0}}[V^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}}}(s)].

Preference Feedback. The agent has access to a panel of PP homogeneous preference panelists. The agent can choose two batches of trajectories 𝒟0={τ0,i}i=0D{\mathcal{D}}_{0}=\{\tau_{0,i}\}_{i=0}^{D} and 𝒟1={τ1,i}i=1D{\mathcal{D}}_{1}=\{\tau_{1,i}\}_{i=1}^{D}, each of which containing DD trajectories, to query preferences (one-bit feedback op∈{0,1}o^{p}\in\{0,1\}), from each panelist p=1,2,….Pp=1,2,\dots.P, where 00 means 𝒟0{\mathcal{D}}_{0} is preferred and 11 means 𝒟1{\mathcal{D}}_{1} is preferred. We assume a utility-based generation mechanism. Specifically, a panelist generates the preference according to a preference model characterized by a link function σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) of the average reward difference between trajectories:

ℙ⁡(op=1)=σ⁡(1D​∑i=1Dr⁡(τi,1)−1D​∑i=1Dr⁡(τi,0)).\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}(o^{p}=1)=\sigma\left(\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=1}^{D}r(\tau_{i,1})-\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=1}^{D}r(\tau_{i,0})\right).

Most preference-based RL works assume either the Bradley-Terry model, in which σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is a standard logistic function [5], or a linear model, in which σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is a linear function [2]. We assume a general and unknown link function and the agent receives a one-bit preference feedback [21]. Note that a panel contains PP panelists, and the panel’s preference oo follows the majority vote among panelists: o=𝟙{∑p=1Pop>P2},o=\mathbbm{1}\{\sum_{p=1}^{P}o^{p}>\frac{P}{2}\}, where 𝟙​{⋅}\mathbbm{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function. The panel preference feedback oo can also be characterized by a link function denoted by σP\sigma_{P},

ℙ⁡(o=1)=ℙ⁡(∑p=1Pop>P2)=σP​(1D​∑i=1Dr⁡(τi,1)−1D​∑i=1Dr⁡(τi,0)).{\mathbb{P}}(o=1)={\mathbb{P}}\left(\sum_{p=1}^{P}o^{p}>\frac{P}{2}\right)=\sigma_{P}\left(\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=1}^{D}r(\tau_{i,1})-\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=1}^{D}r(\tau_{i,0})\right).

σP\sigma_{P} is uniquely determined by σ.\sigma. Larger PP, having more panelists in a panel, increases the accuracy of the preference, and the link function σP\sigma_{P} will be closer to a step function.

2.2 Notations

Let 𝒆i∈ℝd{\bm{e}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} represent the unit vector with all zero elements but 11 on the ii-th coordinate. For a scalar aa, we use sign⁡[a]\sign[a] to denote the sign of the scalar, i.e., sign⁡[a]=1\sign[a]=1 if a>0a>0, sign⁡[a]=−1\sign[a]=-1 if a<0a<0, and sign⁡[0]=0\sign[0]=0. For a vector 𝒗{\bm{v}}, sign⁡[𝒗]\sign[{\bm{v}}] represents the vector after applying the sign\sign operator entry-wise. We use ⊤\top to denote the transpose. To analyze the partial parameters, we introduce the mask vector and the Hadamard product operator. Given a coordinate indices subset ℐ⊆{1,2,…,d}{\mathcal{I}}\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,d\}, we define the binary mask vector 𝒆ℐ∈{0,1}d\bm{e}_{{\mathcal{I}}}\in\{0,1\}^{d} whose ii-th entry is 11 if i∈ℐi\in{\mathcal{I}}, and 00 otherwise. The Hadamard product 𝒂∘𝒃\bm{a}\circ\bm{b} of two vectors 𝒂\bm{a} and 𝒃\bm{b} is the entry-wise product of 𝒂\bm{a} and 𝒃\bm{b}. Hence, for any given vector 𝒂∈ℝd\bm{a}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, 𝒂∘𝒆ℐ\bm{a}\circ\bm{e}_{{\mathcal{I}}} is the masked vector with the entries of 𝒂\bm{a} not in ℐ{{\mathcal{I}}} being 00.

2.3 Partitioned Federated Reinforcement Learning (ParFed-RL)

In this section, we introduce the partitioned federated reinforcement learning (ParFed-RL) framework as shown in Figure 1, which consists of a central server and KK agents. Each agent interacts with their respective local environment to collect trajectories. Then, it queries the local preference panelists for preference feedback over pairs of trajectory batches. Note that in the existing federated reinforcement learning algorithms [6], each agent computes an update direction and communicates it to the server, and the server aggregates the updates, e.g., by averaging, and updates the model. In ParFed-RL, each agent is responsible for updating just a subset of parameters instead of computing an update direction for the entire parameter vector. In particular, assuming the parameter 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} is dd-dimensional, ParFed-RL partitions it into KK equal-sized blocks, 𝜽=[𝜽(1),⋯,𝜽(K)]⊤{\bm{\theta}}=[{\bm{\theta}}^{(1)},\cdots,{\bm{\theta}}^{(K)}]^{\top}, where each 𝜽(k)∈ℝd/K{\bm{\theta}}^{(k)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d/K} is a block of parameters. Agent kk then computes a partial ascent direction 𝒗k∘𝒆ℐk,{{\bm{v}}}_{k}\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}, where ℐk{\mathcal{I}}_{k} is the index set of the assigned parameter block to agent k,k, and broadcasts it. The server and all agents then update their actors with learning rate α:\alpha:

𝜽←𝜽+α​∑k𝒗k∘𝒆ℐk.\bm{\theta}\leftarrow\bm{\theta}+\alpha\sum_{k}{{\bm{v}}}_{k}\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}.

If we let 𝒗k∘𝒆ℐk{{\bm{v}}}_{k}\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}} be the partial gradient, then this becomes a multi-agent version of the policy-gradient algorithm. However, computing the gradient is both computationally and memory-intensive, and communicating the exact gradients also requires significant bandwidth. We next present a ParFed-RL algorithm that is based on stochastic zeroth-order policy optimization with binary perturbation and has low communication overhead and low computation and memory complexity.

3 Algorithm

In this section, we introduce Par-S2ZPO, which stands for Partitioned, Sign-based Stochastic Zeroth-order Policy Optimization. The algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1.

At each iteration tt, Par-S2ZPO consists of the following key steps:

  1. 1.

    Perturbation Sampling. The central server generates a dd-dimensional parameter perturbation vector 𝒗t{\bm{v}}_{t}, where each element is independently sampled from a symmetric binary distribution over {−1,1}\{-1,1\}, i.e., a Rademacher distribution, which will be broadcast to all agents.

  2. 2.

    Policy Perturbation. After receiving 𝒗t,{\bm{v}}_{t}, agent kk perturbs the subset of parameters it is responsible for based on 𝒗t{\bm{v}}_{t} to obtain a perturbed policy actor 𝜽t,k{\bm{\theta}}_{t,k}.

  3. 3.

    Policy Evaluation. For both policies 𝜽t{\bm{\theta}}_{t} and 𝜽t,k{\bm{\theta}}_{t,k}, agent kk interacts with the environment to sample multiple batches of trajectories and queries the local preference panel to obtain the preference over policies (O^t,k∈{−1,1}\hat{{O}}_{t,k}\in\{-1,1\}) through a majority vote. The mechanism is shown in Algorithm 2.

  4. 4.

    Preference Aggregation and Policy Update. After each agent broadcasts the policy preference O^t,k\hat{{O}}_{t,k}, the central server and all agents compute the binary policy parameter update direction by stacking the signed perturbation vector, i.e.,

    𝒈^t=∑k=1KO^t,k​(𝒗t∘𝒆ℐk),\displaystyle\hat{{\bm{g}}}_{t}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{{O}}_{t,k}\left({\bm{v}}_{t}\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}\right),

    and obtain a new actor via update 𝜽t+1=𝜽t+αt​𝒈^t.{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}={\bm{\theta}}_{t}+\alpha_{t}\hat{{\bm{g}}}_{t}.

The design of Par-S2ZPO has two ingredients: partition of the parameters, zeroth-order optimization with binary perturbation.

Zeroth-order optimization with binary perturbation: To avoid communicating and storing real-valued gradients, Par-S2ZPO is based on zeroth-order optimization [13], where the key idea is estimating the gradient by the value comparison between two points by perturbing 𝒙{\bm{x}} to 𝒙+μ​𝒗{\bm{x}}+\mu{\bm{v}}:

∇f​(𝒙)≈c0​𝔼𝒗​[sign⁡[f⁡(𝒙+μ​𝒗)−f⁡(𝒙)]​𝒗].\nabla f({\bm{x}})\approx c_{0}~\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{v}}}\left[\sign[f({\bm{x}}+\mu{\bm{v}})-f({\bm{x}})]{\bm{v}}\right].

Par-S2ZPO uses binary perturbation instead of Gaussian perturbation, so it is communication efficient. Since it is a gradient-free property, it further reduces computation and memory complexity.

Parameter Partition: The federated learning framework enables the collaboration among distributed agents in training one RL model together. To further leverage the diversity of different agents, Par-S2ZPO partitions the parameter set into KK subsets and each agent focuses on evaluating the advantage of the subset perturbation, which gives 2K2^{K} possible directions, i.e., (±𝒗t,1,±𝒗t,2,⋯,±𝒗t,K)(\pm{\bm{v}}_{t,1},\pm{\bm{v}}_{t,2},\cdots,\pm{\bm{v}}_{t,K}) instead of 22 directions, ±𝒗t\pm{\bm{v}}_{t} in the centralized case.

4 Main Results

In this section, we quantify the convergence rate of Par-S2ZPO.

4.1 Definitions and Assumptions

To measure the performance of Par-S2ZPO, which updates the actor network block-wise, we first define the block-sum norm.

Definition 1

(Block-sum norm) For any dd-dimension vector 𝐯∈ℝd{\bm{v}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, given a partition of the coordinate indices 𝒫K={ℐk}k=1K{\mathcal{P}}_{K}=\{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} with KK subsets, we define the block-sum norm as:

‖𝒗‖𝒫K:=∑k=1K∑i∈ℐkvi2,\left\|{\bm{v}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}:=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}v_{i}^{2}},

where viv_{i} is the ii-th entry of 𝐯{\bm{v}}.

Proposition 1

The block-sum norm ‖⋅‖𝒫K\left\|\cdot\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}} is a norm in ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, i.e.,

  1. 1.

    for any 𝒙,𝒚{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}, ‖𝒙+𝒚‖𝒫K≤‖𝒙‖𝒫K+‖𝒚‖𝒫K.\left\|{\bm{x}}+{\bm{y}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\leq\left\|{\bm{x}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}+\left\|{\bm{y}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}.

  2. 2.

    for any 𝒙{\bm{x}} and scalar aa, ‖a​𝒙‖𝒫K=|a|⋅‖𝒙‖𝒫K.\left\|a{\bm{x}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}=|a|\cdot\left\|{\bm{x}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}.

  3. 3.

    for 𝒙{\bm{x}}, if ‖𝒙‖𝒫K=0\left\|{\bm{x}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}=0, then 𝒙=𝟎{\bm{x}}=\bm{0}.

Proposition 2

Given a partition of the coordinate indices 𝒫K{\mathcal{P}}_{K},

‖𝒗‖2≤‖𝒗‖𝒫K≤K​‖𝒗‖2,∀𝒗∈ℝd.\left\|{\bm{v}}\right\|_{2}\leq\left\|{\bm{v}}\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\leq\sqrt{K}\left\|{\bm{v}}\right\|_{2},\quad\forall{\bm{v}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}.

These two propositions can be easily proved via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. We then assume the value function in our problem is smooth, which is a popular assumption used in analyzing deep learning algorithms [3, 4, 1] and RL algorithms [15, 20].

Assumption 1

The value function V⁡(π𝛉)V\left(\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\right) is LL-smooth, i.e., it satisfies

‖∇θV​(π𝜽1)−∇θV​(π𝜽2)‖2≤L​‖𝜽1−𝜽2‖2\left\|\nabla_{\theta}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{1}}\right)-\nabla_{\theta}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{2}}\right)\right\|_{2}\leq L\left\|{\bm{\theta}}_{1}-{\bm{\theta}}_{2}\right\|_{2}

The smoothness assumption implies that a small perturbation in the parameters results in only a small change in the value function. Under this assumption, the panelists may find it difficult to distinguish between two policies by just comparing a finite batch of trajectories when their values are close to each other. To model this, we introduce distinguishability, which characterizes the limitation of the human preference when evaluating finite batches [21].

Definition 2

(Distinguishability) Let DD be the batch size, and ςP​(x)=σP​(x)−12\varsigma_{P}\left(x\right)=\sigma_{P}\left(x\right)-\frac{1}{2} be the preference deviation function. The distinguishability, ϵD∗>0,\epsilon_{D}^{*}>0, is the maximum constant ϵ\epsilon such that for any two policies π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2} with V⁡(π1)−V⁡(π2)>ϵV\left(\pi_{1}\right)-V\left(\pi_{2}\right)>\epsilon,

𝔼𝒟1∼π1,𝒟2∼π2​[ςP​(r¯​(𝒟1)−r¯​(𝒟2))]≥12​ςP​(V⁡(π1)−V⁡(π2)2).\mathbb{E}_{{\mathcal{D}}_{1}\sim\pi_{1},{\mathcal{D}}_{2}\sim\pi_{2}}\left[\varsigma_{P}\left(\bar{r}\left({\mathcal{D}}_{1}\right)-\bar{r}\left({\mathcal{D}}_{2}\right)\right)\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\varsigma_{P}\left(\frac{V\left(\pi_{1}\right)-V\left(\pi_{2}\right)}{2}\right).}

where 𝒟1{\mathcal{D}}_{1} and 𝒟2{\mathcal{D}}_{2} are trajectory batches with size DD sampled under policies π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2}, and r¯\bar{r} returns to the averaged rewards over trajectories in one batch.

This distinguishability characterizes the fundamental limit of using preferences over finite-size batches to recover the true preference between two policies because 𝔼⁡[ςP​(X)]≠ςP​(𝔼⁡[X])\mathbb{E}\left[\varsigma_{P}(X)\right]\not=\varsigma_{P}(\mathbb{E}[X]) in general. While the inequality always holds when D→∞,D\rightarrow\infty, it is possible that when DD is not large enough, the panel cannot reliably tell which policy is better from finite-size batches when the value functions of the two policies are too close, even with infinitely many panelists. ϵD∗\epsilon^{*}_{D} defines this fundamental limit with a given D.D.

4.2 Rate of Convergence

We present an upper bound on the convergence rate of Par-S2ZPO.

Theorem 1

Assume time-homogeneous perturbation distance, i.e, μt=μ\mu_{t}=\mu for all tt, and learning rates αt=Θ⁡(H/d​t)\alpha_{t}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{{H}/{dt}}\right). After TT policy iterations under Par-S2ZPO, if we sample policy 𝛉R{\bm{\theta}}_{R} from {𝛉t}t=1T\{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} with probability ℙ⁡(𝛉R=𝛉i)=αi/∑t=1Tαt{\mathbb{P}}\left({\bm{\theta}}_{R}={\bm{\theta}}_{i}\right)={\alpha_{i}}/{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{t}}, the following holds:

𝔼⁡[‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)‖𝒫K]=𝒪~​(H​dT+μ​d+ϵD∗​Kμ+Kμ​ςP−1​(4N)).\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\right]=\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{Hd}{T}}+\mu d+\frac{\epsilon^{*}_{D}K}{\mu}+\frac{K}{\mu}\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)\right).

Recall that HH is the planning horizon, dd is the parameter dimension, TT is the number of policy iterations, ϵD∗\epsilon_{D}^{*} is the distinguishability, KK is the number of agents, NN is the number of batch pairs per policy iteration sampled by each agent, and ςP​(x)\varsigma_{P}\left(x\right) is the preference deviation function. Since ∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t)=0\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)=0 implies that the policy optimization reaches a stationary point, the inequality above provides an upper bound on the rate of convergence in terms of the number of policy iterations T.T. The detailed proof of Theorem 1 can be found in Section 4.3. The upper bound consists of three parts.

  • •

    The first part 𝒪~​(H​d/T+μ​d)\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}(\sqrt{{Hd}/{T}}+\mu d) is due to stochastic zeroth-order optimization, which is positively correlated to the perturbation distance μ.\mu. This is because by considering a perturbed policy that is μ\mu-distance away, the algorithm misses better policies that are closer than the perturbation distance.

  • •

    The second part 𝒪~​(ϵD∗​K/μ)\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}({\epsilon^{*}_{D}K}/{\mu}) is due to the distinguishability of human feedback defined in Definition 2 and the third part in the theorem 𝒪~​(K​ςP−1​(4/N)/μ)\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}({K}\varsigma_{P}^{-1}(\sqrt{{4}/{N}})/{\mu}) is a result of the majority vote error, both inverse proportional to the perturbation distance μ\mu. When the two policies are closer, their value difference becomes smaller. Since human panelists can only access a finite number of trajectory samples, the difference between the two values may become too small for the panelists to distinguish.

From Theorem 1, by tuning the perturbation distance μ\mu, we can obtain the following upper bound.

Corollary 1

Choosing the perturbation distance μ\mu such that μ2=Θ⁡(K/d​max⁡{ςP−1​(4/N),ϵD∗}),\mu^{2}=\Theta({K}/{d}\max\{\varsigma_{P}^{-1}(\sqrt{{4}/{N}}),\epsilon^{*}_{D}\}), Theorem 1 becomes:

𝔼⁡[‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)‖𝒫K]=d⋅𝒪~​(HT+ϵD∗​K+K​ςP−1​(4N)).\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\right]=\sqrt{d}\cdot\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{H}{T}}+\sqrt{\epsilon^{*}_{D}K}+\sqrt{K\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)}\right). (1)

From this corollary, we can have some interesting observations. Consider the case where dd is large and KK subsets are generated randomly and independently at each iteration. Then, with a high probability, we have

‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)∘𝒆ℐk‖2≈‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)∘𝒆ℐh‖2,∀k,h∈[K]\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}\right\|_{2}\approx\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{h}}\right\|_{2},\quad\forall k,h\in[K]

or

‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)‖𝒫K≈K​‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)‖2.\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\right\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}\approx\sqrt{K}\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\right\|_{2}.

Substituting this into Equation (1), we have

𝔼⁡[‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)‖2]=d⋅𝒪~​(HT​K+ϵD∗+ςP−1​(4N)).\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\right\|_{2}\right]=\sqrt{d}\cdot\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{H}{TK}}+\sqrt{\epsilon^{*}_{D}}+\sqrt{\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)}\right). (2)

Recall that at each iteration, each agent samples 2​N​D2ND trajectories for obtaining preferences. So over TT iterations, the algorithm samples 2​N​D​K​T2NDKT trajectories in total. Let M=2​N​D​K​TM=2NDKT denote the total number of trajectories and let MM measure sample complexity. Then for given MM and K,K, the algorithm can iterates T=M2​N​D​KT=\frac{M}{2NDK} iterations. Substituting MM into the upper bound (2) yields

𝔼⁡[‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽R)‖2]=d⋅𝒪~​(2​N​D​HM+ϵD∗+ςP−1​(4N)).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{R}}\right)\right\|_{2}\right]=\sqrt{d}\cdot\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2NDH}{M}}+\sqrt{\epsilon^{*}_{D}}+\sqrt{\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)}\right). (3)

We can make two observations from this upper bound:

  • •

    The upper bound is independent of K.K. In other words, sample-wise, KK-agent system is as efficient as a centralized, single-agent system (K=1K=1), even though the single-agent system takes KK times more iterations under the same sample complexity. Our simulations will confirm this observation.

  • •

    There is a tradeoff in choosing D,D, the batch size, The first term 2​D​H/M\sqrt{{2DH}/{M}} is positively correlated to DD, whereas the second term ϵD∗\sqrt{\epsilon_{D}^{*}} is inversely correlated to DD (with common human preference models, we have ϵD∗=O~​(H/D)\epsilon_{D}^{*}=\tilde{O}(H/\sqrt{D}) [21]). A larger batch size DD will decrease the total training iterations while making each training iteration more accurate. There is also a tradeoff in choosing N,N, similar to that of D.D.

4.3 Proof of Theorem 1

In this section, we prove Theorem 1 from a Lyapunov drift analysis framework. We start by analyzing the drift of the value function between successive policy iterations, i.e., V⁡(π𝜽t+1)−V⁡(π𝜽t)V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}}\right)-V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right).

Recall that by assumption, the value function V⁡(π𝜽t)V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right) is LL-smooth, so we can linearize the drift up to a second-order error, which is characterized by the following lemma:

Lemma 1

(Lemma 7 in [10]) For any LL-smooth function f:ℝd→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}, and ∀𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd\forall{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, we have:

|f⁡(𝒚)−f⁡(𝒙)−⟨∇f​(𝒙),𝒚−𝒙⟩|≤L2​‖𝒚−𝒙‖22.|f\left({\bm{y}}\right)-f\left({\bm{x}}\right)-\left\langle\nabla f\left({\bm{x}}\right),{\bm{y}}-{\bm{x}}\right\rangle|\leq\frac{L}{2}\left\|{\bm{y}}-{\bm{x}}\right\|_{2}^{2}.

Substituting in the value function V⁡(π𝜽t)V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right), we bound the drift as:

V⁡(π𝜽t+1)−V⁡(π𝜽t)\displaystyle V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}}\right)-V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)
≥\displaystyle\geq ⟨∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t),𝜽t+1−𝜽t⟩−L2​‖𝜽t+1−𝜽t‖22\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\rangle-\frac{L}{2}\|{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}
=\displaystyle= αt​⟨∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t),𝒈^t⟩−L​αt22​‖𝒈^t‖22\displaystyle\alpha_{t}\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),\hat{{{\bm{g}}}}_{t}\rangle-\frac{L\alpha_{t}^{2}}{2}\|\hat{{{\bm{g}}}}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}
=\displaystyle= αt​∑k=1K⟨∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t),O^t,k​𝒗t,k⟩−L​αt22​‖∑k=1KO^t,k​𝒗t,k‖22,\displaystyle\alpha_{t}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),\hat{{O}}_{t,k}{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\rangle-\frac{L\alpha_{t}^{2}}{2}\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{{O}}_{t,k}{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\right\|_{2}^{2},

where the first equality uses the gradient ascent update and the second equality uses the definition of the gradient estimator 𝒈^t\hat{{{\bm{g}}}}_{t} in Algorithm 1. Since the panelists’ decision, i.e., O^t,k\hat{{O}}_{t,k}, is related to the value difference between policies before and after perturbation, each inner product can be decomposed as follows:

⟨∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t),O^t,k​𝒗t,k⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),\hat{{O}}_{t,k}{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\right\rangle
=\displaystyle= ⟨∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t),sign⁡[V⁡(π𝜽t,k′)−V⁡(π𝜽t)]​𝒗t,k⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),\operatorname{sign}\left[V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t,k}^{\prime}}\right)-V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\right]{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\right\rangle
+⟨∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t),(O^t,k−sign⁡[V⁡(π𝜽t,k′)−V⁡(π𝜽t)])​𝒗t,k⟩.\displaystyle+\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),\left(\hat{{O}}_{t,k}-\operatorname{sign}\left[V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t,k}^{\prime}}\right)-V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\right]\right){{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\right\rangle.

The first term characterizes how the gradient direction of ∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t)\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right) aligns with the value difference sign between the perturbed and the original policy, and the second term quantifies the error of approximating the value difference sign with the majority vote from NN trajectories. The following two lemmas bound the conditional expectation of these two terms separately.

Lemma 2

Let ℱt{\mathcal{F}}_{t} be the filtration up to the tt-th iteration, we have:

𝔼[⟨∇𝜽V(π𝜽t),sign[V(π𝜽t,k′)−V(π𝜽t)]𝒗t,k⟩|ℱt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left.\left\langle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right),\operatorname{sign}\left[V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t,k}^{\prime}}\right)-V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\right]{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\right\rangle\right|{\mathcal{F}}_{t}\right]

The error of the majority vote is bounded as:

≤2e2​‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t)∘𝒆ℐk‖2+2​(μt​L​|ℐk|+ϵD∗μt)+8μt​ςP−1​(4N).\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{e^{2}}\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}\right\|_{2}+2\left(\mu_{t}L|{\mathcal{I}}_{k}|+\frac{\epsilon^{*}_{D}}{\mu_{t}}\right)+\frac{8}{\mu_{t}}\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right).

The proofs of Lemma 2 and Lemma 3 are deferred to the appendix. Collecting these two bounds, we can lower bound the conditional expectation of the first term in the drift as follows:

≥\displaystyle\geq (13−2e2)​∑k=1K‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t)∘𝒆ℐk‖2\displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{2}{e^{2}}\right)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\circ{{\bm{e}}}_{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}}\|_{2}
−∑k=1K(3μL|ℐk|+2​ϵD∗μ+8μςP−1(4N))\displaystyle-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(3\mu L|{\mathcal{I}}_{k}|+\frac{2\epsilon^{*}_{D}}{\mu}+\frac{8}{\mu}\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)\right)
≥\displaystyle\geq 14​‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t)‖𝒫K−8​(μ​L​d+ϵD∗​Kμ+Kμ​ςP−1​(4N)),\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}-8\left(\mu Ld+\frac{\epsilon^{*}_{D}K}{\mu}+\frac{K}{\mu}\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)\right),

where the last step uses ∑k=1K|ℐk|=d\sum_{k=1}^{K}|{\mathcal{I}}_{k}|=d since {ℐk}k=1K\{{\mathcal{I}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} is a partition of coordinates. Next, we bound the second-order approximation error in the drift. Notice that for a different agent kk, the perturbation vector 𝒗t,k{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k} is either −1-1 or 11 on the coordinates in ℐk{\mathcal{I}}_{k} and 00 at other entries. So for another agent ll, the ℐl{\mathcal{I}}_{l} entries in vector 𝒗t,k{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k} should all be zero, which means the inner product of 𝒗t,k{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k} and 𝒗t,l{{\bm{v}}}_{t,l} should be 00. Then, the second-order error is simply the following:

‖∑k=1KO^t,k​𝒗t,k‖22=∑k=1KO^t,k2​‖𝒗t,k‖22=∑k=1K|ℐk|=d.\displaystyle\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{{O}}_{t,k}{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{{O}}_{t,k}^{2}\|{{\bm{v}}}_{t,k}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}|{\mathcal{I}}_{k}|=d.

Therefore, collecting the bounds of both terms in the drift analysis, we have:

𝔼⁡[V⁡(π𝜽t)−V⁡(π𝜽t+1)|ℱt]≤−αt4​‖∇𝜽V​(π𝜽t)‖𝒫K+αt2​L​d2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)-V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}}\right)|{\mathcal{F}}_{t}\right]\leq-\frac{\alpha_{t}}{4}\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}V\left(\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}}\right)\|_{{\mathcal{P}}_{K}}+\frac{\alpha_{t}^{2}Ld}{2}

+∑t=1T8αt(μLd+ϵD∗​Kμ+KμςP−1(4N))+∑t=1Tαt2L​d2.\displaystyle+\sum_{t=1}^{T}8\alpha_{t}\left(\mu Ld+\frac{\epsilon^{*}_{D}K}{\mu}+\frac{K}{\mu}\varsigma_{P}^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4}{N}}\right)\right)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{t}^{2}\frac{Ld}{2}.

5 Experiments

This section presents the performance of Par-S2ZPO in four Mujoco environments [18]: Half Cheetah, Hopper, Swimmer, and Walker2D. In Mujoco environments, RL policies take the robots’ positions and postures (observations) as input, and output the forces and torques to control the robots to accomplish the tasks. The performances are measured by the accumulated rewards defined by the environments.

All policies are parameterized by neural networks (actor networks) with two hidden layers of size 64, while input and output dimensions depend on the environment. Each actor is first pretrained using PPO [17], providing a stable and stochastic initialization for further zeroth-order fine-tuning. The preference model of each panelist is a linear link function

σ⁡(x)=max⁡{0,min⁡{a​x+0.5,1}},a=0.01.\sigma(x)=\max\{0,\min\{ax+0.5,1\}\},\quad a=0.01.

Each agent is associated with a panel of P=100P=100 panelists. For each query, the panel samples one pair of trajectory batches (N=1N=1), collects individual preferences, and returns the majority vote. The underlying rewards and link function are unknown to the agents. Each experiment is initialized with learning rate α=0.01\alpha=0.01 and perturbation magnitude d=0.05d=0.05. At each policy iteration, after receiving feedback from all agents, a server-side panel (identical to agent panels) evaluates whether the updated policy would be preferred over the current one. The update is accepted only if preferred; otherwise, it is rejected. If three consecutive rejections occur, both α\alpha and dd are halved. If the updated policy is accepted, Adam [8] with gradient clipping was then used. When evaluating the performance of a policy at each iteration, we use 2020 new episodes.

Our experiments focus on the following aspects: (1) the impact of batch size D,D, (2) the impact of the number of agents K,K, (3) binary versus Gaussian perturbation, and (4) performance comparison with the FedAvg-type of federated learning framework.

Batch size DD selection

The upper bound (3) reveals a tradeoff in batch size DD. The different choices of DD’s can be explained by the distinguishability ϵD∗\epsilon_{D}^{*}, which is a decreasing function of DD. Under a fixed sample complexity, when ϵD∗\epsilon_{D}^{*} is already relatively small, continuing to increase DD can result in a decrease in the total training iteration, which is wasteful and impacts the training performance.

In Figure 2, we plotted the empirical distributions of the average returns of DD trajectories of the policies before and after perturbation. For Half Cheetah, Swimmer and Walker 2D, we sampled 500500 batches per policy, and for Hopper, we sampled 150150 batches per policy.

We can observe that for Hopper, the two policies are already well separated at D=1D=1, so ϵD∗\epsilon_{D}^{*} is sufficiently small even with D=1D=1. For Swimmer, increasing DD reduces the overlap between the two distributions, but the separation is clear even when D=1D=1. Therefore, increasing DD provides no additional benefit and only reduces the number of policy iterations. For Half Cheetah and Walker 2D, the empirical distributions of the policies before and after perturbation have significant overlap, which decreases significantly when DD increases from 1 to 4. Therefore, increasing DD improves distinguishability significantly, which leads to the tradeoff in the upper bound (3). In the following experiments, for Hopper and Swimmer, we select D=1D=1, and for Half Cheetah and Walker 2D, we select D=4D=4.

Agent size KK study

In this experiment, we studied the performance of Par-S2ZPO with different values of K=1, 5, 10, 15K=1,\ 5,\ 10,\ 15 under the sample complexity. i.e., the training iteration decreases proportionally with the increase of KK. We repeated the training 2020 times for each KK. The training performances with standard deviations are shown in Table 1. From the table, we can observe that after considering the standard deviations, the performance remains the same across different KK’s, which is consistent with Section 4.2.

Binary versus Gaussian perturbations

Our binary perturbation leads to low communication, computation, and memory complexity. In this experiment, we compared the performances of the binary and Gaussian perturbations. From each environment, we choose the agent size K=1K=1 to compare the two perturbations. We set the training iteration T=150T=150 for Half Cheetah, Swimmer, and Walker 2D, and T=30T=30 for Hopper since the training in Hopper converges faster. The comparison is shown in the first two columns of Table 1, which indicates that the two perturbation methods have similar performance. This justifies our choice of binary perturbation.

Performance comparison with FedAvg

In this experiment, we compared Par-S2ZPO with FedAvg-S2ZPO. We used K=5K=5 distributed agents. Each method is run for 20 independent trials, and results with standard errors are reported in Figure 3. As shown in Figure 3, Par-S2ZPO consistently outperforms FedAvg-S2ZPO across all environments. Par-S2ZPO partitions the model into K=5K=5 components and independently selects perturbation directions, effectively choosing from 2K=322^{K}=32 potential updates. This enables finer and more efficient policy improvement. For FedAvg-S2ZPO, each agent selects its locally preferred update, and the server averages these updates. This aggregation leads to a coarser update compared to the combinatorial selection in Par-S2ZPO.

Besides a better performance, Par-S2ZPO is more communication- and memory-efficient. In each iteration, FedAvg-S2ZPO requires transmitting KK full-network perturbations, whereas Par-S2ZPO transmits only one perturbation split across KK partitions, reducing communication cost by a factor of KK. Under FedAvg-S2ZPO, each agent must store two full actor networks (original and perturbed) for inference, while Par-S2ZPO requires only one full network and the partial network corresponding to its perturbation partition. For K=5K=5, this reduces storage by approximately 40%40\%.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed Par-S2S^{2}ZPO for Federated RLHF. The algorithm is communication-, computation-, and memory-efficient. The upper bound on the rate of convergence sheds light on the algorithm’s efficiency. Our empirical results confirmed the observations from our theoretical analysis.
